newsitem.title: POLAND: Former Yeltsin aide extradition could take months.
newsitem.headline: Former Yeltsin aide extradition could take months.

text.p: Warsaw prosecutors said on Monday that extraditing former senior Moscow official Sergei Stankevich back to Russia to face corruption charges could take months.

Polish police, acting on an international wanted notice issued by Russia, on Friday arrested the former Moscow deputy mayor who was once a prominent advisor to Russian president Boris Yeltsin but now stands accused of taking bribes.
Ryszard Kucinski, spokesman for the Warsaw provincial prosecutors said Stankevich had been placed under arrest in Warsaw until May 17.
"During this time we will await an extradition application from the Russian side and after we get this, the formal extradition process will be begun," Kucinski told Reuters.

He said the Warsaw provincial court would give its opinion and if the ruling was challenged the case could then go to the appeal court, before the prosecutor-general took a decision whether to extradite Stankevich or not.
He said the process might take some months, depending on how quickly Russia applied and whether the case went to appeal.
"Even if Stankevich said now: 'I want to return to Russia', we would go through the whole extradition process anyway," Kucinski said.
Kucinski, without giving details, said Stankevich had been held on a notice, "concerning the gaining of material benefit, taking bribes, in connection with fulfilling a public function."
Early last year, Moscow prosecutors said Stankevich was being sought on a charge of accepting a $10,000 bribe in 1992 while, as deputy mayor, organising a Red Square music concert.
Stankevich, who advised Yeltsin on political affairs before joining the Moscow city council, had earlier escaped prosecution because he had immunity as a parliamentary deputy.
But he disappeared from view around the time in 1995 that he failed to be re-elected to the State Duma (lower house).
Polish newspapers reported that he had first gone to the United States and had since been in Poland.
Polish prosecutors said Stankevich had appointed a local legal representative but did not identify the lawyer.
The best-selling daily Gazeta Wyborcza reported on Monday that Stankevich had declined to speak to Polish police and agreed only to talk with the security service, UOP.
He said he had been wrongly accused of taking a 5,000 pounds bribe from a London association, the daily said.
